title: Kali Gandaki: Ridi, Rani Mahal and Devghat
meta_description: Kali Gandaki sacred river in 5 nights: Tansen, Rani Mahal palace, the Rishikesh temple at Ridi and the Devghat confluence, ending in Chitwan.
summary: Five nights following Nepal's holiest western river through the hills of Palpa. Base in Tansen for Rani Mahal, sleep beside the Kali Gandaki at the pilgrim bazaar of Ridi, then follow the river's waters down to Devghat, where it meets the Trishuli to form the Narayani. Finish with a night at the edge of Chitwan National Park.
intro: The Kali Gandaki rises near the Tibetan border in Mustang, cuts one of the deepest gorges on earth between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, and then turns through the middle hills of western Nepal before it reaches the plains. For Hindus it is sacred along its whole length. Its bed yields the black ammonite fossils called saligram, worshipped as Vishnu, and its banks hold pilgrimage places that most visitors never see. This journey follows its middle course.

We start in Tansen, the old hill capital of Palpa, and go down to Rani Mahal, the riverside palace a Rana governor built for his late wife. Then Ridi, a bazaar of temples and ghats at the meeting of the Ridi Khola and the Kali Gandaki, where pilgrims come in thousands for Makar Sankranti. Last comes Devghat, the confluence with the Trishuli, where elderly Hindus come to spend their final years. Chitwan is the reward at the end.
story: The first two days are in the hills, in a town of Newar traders and Magar villages, with the river always somewhere below in its gorge. Then you go down to it. At Rani Mahal the water is green and wide under the white palace walls. At Ridi you sleep in a small bazaar where the evening sound is temple bells and the river, and where pilgrims bathe at dawn and buy saligram stones on the ghat steps. The next day the river disappears into gorges and you follow it by road to the plains, where at Devghat it meets the Trishuli under a suspension bridge, among ashrams and cremation ghats. The journey ends with rhinos in the grass at Sauraha.
highlights: Rani Mahal, the 1890s Rana palace on the Kali Gandaki often called Nepal's Taj Mahal
The Rishikesh temple at Ridi and its legend of a Vishnu image that ages through the day
Dawn bathing on the ghats at Ridi and the saligram sellers on the steps
Devghat, the confluence of the Kali Gandaki and the Trishuli, with its ashrams and evening prayers
A last night on the edge of Chitwan National Park with a canoe trip on the Rapti

days.title: Fly to Bhairahawa, drive to Tansen
days.move: ≈ 35 min flight · then ≈ 65 km · 2.5 h drive
days.text: Fly from Kathmandu to Gautam Buddha International Airport at Bhairahawa and drive north through Butwal and up the Siddhartha Highway to Tansen. Check in at Hotel Srinagar on the ridge. In the afternoon walk the bazaar with your guide: the Amar Narayan temple of 1806 with its carved roof struts, the great gate of the Tansen Durbar, and the workshops where dhaka cloth is still woven on handlooms. Dinner in town.

days.title: Rani Mahal on the Kali Gandaki
days.move: Full day by jeep on rural roads · short walk down to the river
days.text: Drive out through Magar villages and terraced maize fields towards the Kali Gandaki gorge, then walk down to Rani Mahal. Khadga Shumsher Rana, governor of Palpa, built it in the 1890s in memory of his wife Tej Kumari, and its white walls stand straight above the river. The same Khadga Shumsher later helped locate the Ashoka pillar at Lumbini in 1896. Sit on the terraces, watch the water and return to Tansen in the late afternoon.

days.title: Down to the river at Ridi
days.text: Drive north-west from Tansen through the Palpa hills and drop to Ridi Bazaar at the confluence of the Ridi Khola and the Kali Gandaki. Visit the Rishikesh temple, dedicated to Vishnu; local legend says its image appears as a child in the morning, a youth at midday and an old man by evening. Walk the ghats, where families perform rites for their dead and pilgrims look for saligram stones in the gravel. Stay in a simple local hotel and listen to the river at night.

days.title: Follow the water to Devghat
days.text: Watch the dawn bathers on the Ridi ghats, then drive back through Tansen and down to Butwal, and east along the Mahendra Highway to Narayangarh, a long but easy day on good roads. Check in at a hotel in Narayangarh and drive the few kilometres north to Devghat in the late afternoon. Cross the suspension bridge over the confluence, where the Kali Gandaki and the Trishuli join to become the Narayani, and stay for the evening prayers at the riverside temples.

days.title: Devghat morning, Chitwan afternoon
days.text: Return to Devghat early, when elderly residents of the ashrams bathe and pray at the ghats and the river is calm and misty. Your guide explains why people come here to live out their last years, and how the confluence is honoured in Hindu tradition. Then drive to Sauraha on the edge of Chitwan National Park and check in at Green Park Chitwan. In the afternoon take a dugout canoe on the Rapti river and walk back through the community forest with a naturalist.

days.title: Bharatpur to Kathmandu
days.move: ≈ 15 km · 30 min drive · then ≈ 25 min flight
days.text: Take an early bird walk along the river with your naturalist if you like; the grasslands are busiest with birds in the first hour of light. After breakfast, drive to Bharatpur airport for the short flight to Kathmandu. If you would rather stay longer in Chitwan, add nights for a jeep safari and a Tharu village visit; our Chitwan journeys join easily here. From the plane on a clear morning you can see the line of the Himalaya to the north, from the Annapurnas east to Langtang.

includes: 5 nights twin sharing: 2 at Hotel Srinagar, 1 in a simple hotel at Ridi, 1 in a good hotel in Narayangarh, 1 at Green Park Chitwan
Breakfast daily, plus meals as listed
Private car with driver throughout, and a jeep for the Rani Mahal day
Licensed English-speaking guide throughout, and a naturalist in Chitwan

good_to_know: Ridi has only simple hotels with basic bathrooms; we choose the cleanest available.
Makar Sankranti in mid-January fills Ridi and Devghat with pilgrims; book well ahead if you want to see it.
Ghats at Ridi and Devghat are places of cremation; ask before photographing people and never photograph funerals.
Monsoon landslides can close the hill roads from June to September; we do not run this route then.
Chitwan National Park fees and rules change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is the Kali Gandaki sacred?
faqs.a: Hindus treat the Kali Gandaki as holy along its whole course, partly because its bed yields saligram, black ammonite fossils worshipped as forms of Vishnu. Its upper valley holds Muktinath, sacred to Hindus and Buddhists, and its banks hold pilgrimage places such as Ridi and, at its confluence with the Trishuli, Devghat. Bathing at these places, especially at Makar Sankranti, is believed to purify.

Ridi Bazaar, where the Ridi Khola meets the Kali Gandaki on the borders of Gulmi, Palpa and Syangja, is known for the Rishikesh temple of Vishnu and for its ghats. Local legend says the temple's image changes from child to youth to old man through each day. The Ridi fair at Makar Sankranti in mid-January draws large crowds of pilgrims.

Devghat is a pilgrimage place at the confluence of the Kali Gandaki and the Trishuli, where they join to form the Narayani, a few kilometres north of Narayangarh. It has temples, ashrams and ghats, and many elderly Hindus come to live here in their last years, believing it auspicious to die at a sacred confluence. A suspension bridge crosses the river.

faqs.q: Is Rani Mahal open to visitors?
faqs.a: Rani Mahal has been under restoration in recent years and visitors have been able to see the exterior and parts of the grounds. Access is by rural road and a walk down to the river, which can be blocked by landslides after the monsoon. Check current status before you travel; we confirm conditions before your day trip.

faqs.q: What are the hotels like at Ridi?
faqs.a: Basic. Ridi is a pilgrim bazaar, not a tourist town, and its hotels are small, family-run places with simple rooms and shared or basic private bathrooms. We choose the cleanest available and warn you in advance. The reward is waking up beside the river in a working pilgrimage town. If you prefer, we can return to Tansen instead.

faqs.q: Can I buy a saligram at Ridi?
faqs.a: Saligram stones are sold by vendors on the ghats at Ridi and are bought by pilgrims for home worship. Prices vary widely with size and form. Be aware that some stones are polished or reshaped, and that exporting fossils may be restricted, so check current status before you travel and keep your receipt.

faqs.q: Is this trip suitable for non-Hindus?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors of any faith are welcome at the ghats and most temple courtyards, though some inner shrines are open only to Hindus; your guide will tell you where. Dress modestly, remove shoes where asked and be quiet and respectful near cremation ghats. This route is as much about river, landscape and village life as religion.

faqs.q: When is the best time to do this trip?
faqs.a: October to March. The hill roads are dry, the river is clear and the weather comfortable. Mid-January brings Makar Sankranti, when Ridi and Devghat fill with pilgrims, which is moving but crowded. From June to September monsoon rain and landslides make the roads unreliable, so we do not run the route then.

faqs.q: Can I add more time in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Yes. One night gives you only a canoe ride and a forest walk. Two or three more nights add jeep safaris into the park, a visit to a Tharu village and time to look for rhinos, gharial crocodiles and, with luck, a tiger. We can also swap Green Park for a lodge in Kasara or Meghauli. Ask us for a re-quote.
